questiontext.text: The course VPC has no NAT Gateway. Your EKS node runs in a public subnet with a public IP, and only RDS sits in the private subnets. What is the main reason the node can't simply run in a private subnet?

answer.text: Without a NAT Gateway, nothing in a private subnet can reach ECR or AWS APIs, so the node couldn't pull images or join the cluster
EKS only supports worker nodes in public subnets
RDS only accepts connections from resources in public subnets
Private subnets are billed per hour, while public subnets are free

questiontext.text: dcta-rds-sg allows port 5432 from dcta-app-sg (which your EKS node wears) rather than from IP ranges. Given that the cluster and its node are re-created every session, what is the key benefit?

answer.text: The rule keeps working even though the node and pods get new IP addresses every session, and it only covers resources that wear the app security group
Security-group references are checked faster than IP ranges, so database queries are quicker
RDS does not support IP-range rules on port 5432
It lets the database be reached from the internet, but only by pods

questiontext.text: In infra/20-data you read the DB password with an ephemeral "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" block. Which way of passing it to aws_db_instance works?

answer.text: password_wo (with password_wo_version) — ephemeral values may only go into write-only arguments, which are never saved to state
password — Terraform encrypts it automatically because it came from an ephemeral block
password with sensitive = true on the argument, which keeps it out of state
username — RDS reads the password from Secrets Manager once it knows the user

questiontext.text: On a fresh RDS for PostgreSQL 17 instance, the backend pod logs no pg_hba.conf entry … no encryption. The security groups are correct. What is the cause?

answer.text: RDS for PostgreSQL 15 and later require TLS by default (rds.force_ssl = 1), and the app is connecting without it
Port 5432 is blocked, so the connection falls back to an unencrypted port
The password synced by External Secrets doesn't match the database
The DB subnet group uses public subnets, which RDS refuses

questiontext.text: You built and pushed the backend image from an Apple Silicon Mac with a plain docker build. The pod pulls the image from ECR and then crashes immediately with exec format error. What went wrong?

answer.text: The image was built for arm64, but the node is amd64 — rebuild with --platform linux/amd64 and push a new tag
The start script in the image isn't executable — add chmod +x in the Dockerfile
The node's IAM role can't pull from ECR
The tag is immutable, so Kubernetes refused to overwrite the running container

questiontext.text: Your single t3.medium node reports a pod capacity of 17, and new pods are stuck Pending with Too many pods. Which fix actually raises the limit to 110?

answer.text: Set ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the VPC CNI add-on before the node group is created, then re-create the cluster stack so a new node joins with it on
Set ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the running add-on — the existing node picks it up within a few minutes
Lower the HPA's maxReplicas so fewer pods are created
Give every pod smaller memory requests so more of them fit

questiontext.text: Which trust-policy condition lets only the External Secrets Operator's ServiceAccount assume dcta-eso-irsa?

answer.text: StringEquals on <issuer>:sub = system:serviceaccount:external-secrets:external-secrets and on <issuer>:aud = sts.amazonaws.com
StringLike on <issuer>:sub = system:serviceaccount:*:* with aud = sts.amazonaws.com
StringEquals on <issuer>:aud = sts.amazonaws.com only
No condition — the ServiceAccount annotation already limits who can use the role

questiontext.text: A test pod is already running with the external-secrets ServiceAccount. You then add the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation. The pod's AWS CLI still says Unable to locate credentials. Why?

answer.text: The role variables and token are only injected into pods created after the annotation — re-create the pod
IAM needs up to an hour to trust a newly annotated ServiceAccount
The cluster has no OIDC provider until the first annotated pod starts
The node's IAM role is blocking the pod's role

questiontext.text: The db-credentials ExternalSecret has been syncing fine. You change its remoteRef.key to a secret the IRSA role can't read and apply it. What happens to the existing Kubernetes Secret?

answer.text: It keeps its current data; the ExternalSecret's status reports the access-denied error
ESO deletes it, because the Secret is owned by the ExternalSecret
ESO empties its keys so the app can't use stale credentials
ESO falls back to the node's IAM role and syncs the new secret anyway

questiontext.text: The DB password is rotated in Secrets Manager. ESO refreshes, and kubectl get secret db-credentials shows the new value. The backend (which loads it with envFrom) still fails to log in. What's the fix?

answer.text: Restart the backend Deployment — pods only read environment variables when they start
Lower the ExternalSecret's refreshInterval
Restart the External Secrets Operator
Re-annotate the ServiceAccount so IRSA issues new credentials

questiontext.text: On EKS without any extra load balancer controller, you create a Service of type: LoadBalancer with no annotations. What does AWS create?

answer.text: A Classic Load Balancer — you need service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: nlb to get an NLB
A Network Load Balancer, the default for LoadBalancer Services
An Application Load Balancer, because the Service speaks HTTP
Nothing — EKS can't create load balancers without the AWS Load Balancer Controller

questiontext.text: Your app's Ingress has no host. You add a second Ingress with no host for Grafana, on the same F5 NGINX Ingress Controller. What happens, and what's the fix?

answer.text: Only one host-less Ingress can be the default, so they collide (the older one wins) — give Grafana a host rule instead
NGINX merges both Ingresses' paths automatically — no fix needed
AWS creates a second NLB for the second Ingress
The newer Ingress always wins, so Grafana replaces the app

questiontext.text: You run terraform destroy on 40-track-b-cluster before 41-track-b-platform. What is the main risk?

answer.text: The NLB created by the ingress controller's Service can be left running outside Terraform, because the cluster that should delete it is gone
None — the NLB is in the cluster stack's Terraform state, so it's destroyed with the cluster
Argo CD re-creates the cluster from Git
RDS is deleted too, because it depends on the cluster's security group

questiontext.text: When autoscaling is on, the backend Deployment template leaves out replicas. Argo CD has self-heal on. Why leave it out?

answer.text: Otherwise Argo CD keeps resetting the replica count to the value in Git, fighting the HPA
The HPA refuses to target a Deployment that has a replicas field
Kubernetes ignores replicas whenever an HPA exists, so the field is just noise
It saves a pod slot on the single node

questiontext.text: metrics-server is running and kubectl top pods works, but kubectl get hpa shows TARGETS <unknown>/70% for the backend. What is the most likely cause?

answer.text: The backend container has no CPU request, so the HPA has nothing to measure 70% against
Prometheus isn't installed, and the HPA reads its metrics from Prometheus
maxReplicas is set lower than the current replica count
The monitoring Application needs ServerSideApply=true
